AfriScan · Nigeria · Secure your land from the air, remotely

Know what is changing on your right of way, before the next patrol does

We map the structures, fresh excavations, cleared ground and tracks on the rights of way of your pipelines and power lines in Nigeria, measure each one to the line and show what changed between dated surveys. Satellite first, drone detail under the NCAA and ONSA authorisations each job requires, and a person reviews every result before it reaches you.

The law behind the register Oil Pipelines Act s.12 · Petroleum Industry Act 2021 ss.90, 127, 176 · Land Use Act ss.28–29 · NESIS Regulations 2015 s.3.1 · EIA Act 1992 · Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21 · NDPA 2023 · IFC Performance Standard 5

Already in the law

The setbacks your register is measured against

Nigerian law draws lines along pipelines and power lines. A setback only protects the asset if someone can see what stands inside it, and when it arrived.

Oil Pipelines Act, s.12

Pipelines: up to 100 feet beyond the licence strip

On the licence holder’s application, the President can attach an order to a pipeline licence prohibiting or restricting buildings, cultivation and industrial or mining activity “within a specified distance, not exceeding 100 feet, from the boundaries of the land” in the licence (Oil Pipelines Act). We measure to that distance from the strip you send us.

NESIS Regulations 2015

Power lines: no structures under the line

NERC’s standard sets rights of way of 50 m for 330 kV, 30 m for 132 kV and 11 m for 33 kV and 11 kV lines, divided equally either side of the centre line, and says “no structures shall be built under the Overhead line Right of Way” (NESIS, s.3.1).

Land Use Act, ss.28–29

Compensation: buildings counted at a date

Land can be revoked for “mining purposes or oil pipelines” (s.28), with compensation for buildings at replacement cost less depreciation (s.29(4)) (Land Use Act). A dated record of which structures stood where is what compensation enumeration and an IFC Performance Standard 5 cut-off date are built on.

Why it matters

What changes between patrols

Nigerian trunklines and transmission lines cross swamp, creeks, farmland, savannah and fast-growing towns. The ground beside them changes faster than any patrol cycle can record.

“There are new buildings on the right of way.”

Homes, shops, workshops and fences go up inside setbacks, most often where a line runs beside a road or a town grows towards it. Each one is easier to discuss while it is new and few.

“Someone has been digging near the line.”

Third-party interference shows at the surface as fresh digging, spoil, new footpaths and tracks, and cleared ground. We flag those between surveys so field teams know where to look first.

“Settlement is following the new gas line.”

New trunklines bring access roads, and access roads bring building. A dated baseline taken when the line is laid is the record every later compensation or encroachment discussion goes back to.

“We can’t get to that stretch safely.”

Swamp and creek crossings, remote savannah and insecure areas are slow, costly or unsafe to reach. Satellite screening needs no one on site, so the whole corridor is covered before anyone decides where to send a team.

The operators’ own reports show why the record matters. NNPC’s monthly report for July 2026 tracks “Upstream Pipeline Availability” as a headline measure and lists “pipeline incidents” among the causes of lost crude output (NNPC, July 2026). In June 2026 TCN reported damage to six towers on its Apir–Lafia 330 kV lines (TCN, 2 June 2026). Imagery cannot prevent either; it can show where the ground around the asset has changed, and when.

What you receive

A register your right-of-way, community and GIS teams can use

  • Each structure listed with an ID, its distance to the line, its band, its chainage and its coordinates in WGS84 and in the route’s UTM zone (31N, 32N or 33N in Nigeria).
  • Every 500 m rated high, medium or low for encroachment density, so the right-of-way team knows where to go first.
  • Change between dated surveys: new and removed structures, fresh digging and new tracks, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer.
  • The imagery named, and dated where the source gives a date.
  • A PDF report and GIS layers in GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile, and an interactive map file that opens in a browser, including in the field.

Structures, fresh digging and new tracks on trunkline, delivery-line and product-line rights of way, from the Delta’s creeks to the new gas lines in the north, with visible signs of artisanal refining flagged for checking.

Our standard

Land and assets, never people

AfriScan maps what is on the land: structures, cleared ground, excavations and tracks. We do not identify, count or follow people, and whether a structure is authorised is for you and the authorities to decide. We write “structures”, never “illegal occupants”, and our work is remote sensing and mapping, not a security service.

A person reviews every result

Building datasets and detection models propose; a reviewer confirms, corrects and adds. What the imagery cannot settle is listed for a ground check.

Dated and credited

Every report names its imagery and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Map-service basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery.

Scheduled, never “real‑time”

Satellites and drones capture images on particular dates, so re-surveys follow a schedule agreed with you, with a notice of what changed and where.

Confidential by default

Results go only to the contacts you name. Military and other sensitive sites are masked, and nothing about your assets is published.

Satellite first, drones where the permits allow

Two routes to the picture, and the rules for each

Satellite and your own imagery. A survey starts from your route file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos your own drone teams already fly. No one travels and no drone flies, however long the line. We found no rule that requires a licence to buy or analyse commercial satellite imagery in Nigeria; counsel should confirm it for your project.

Drone detail. Where a stretch needs more detail than satellite imagery shows, a drone survey captures it, subject to the NCAA and ONSA authorisations each job requires. In Nigeria that means an RPAS Operator Certificate, registered drones, ONSA security clearance, End-User Certificates for imported equipment and ATC clearance in controlled airspace, and flights over populated stretches or along high-tension lines need specific approval. Afridrone is working towards the authorisations Nigeria requires, and every drone proposal lists the approvals its flights need and when each must be in place.

The Nigeria drone-law guide

The NCAA approvals, ONSA clearance, the End-User Certificate, the rules along a right of way, the NDPA and a 15-point checklist for anyone commissioning a drone survey, with sources, as of 26 September 2026.

Drone law in Nigeria

For procurement and compliance teams

Nigerian content, registrations and tenders

Oil and gas contracts in Nigeria run under the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry Content Development Act 2010, with registration on NOGIC JQS, NUPRC service permits for upstream contractors and NCDMB approval of larger contracting processes. Federal buyers such as TCN procure under the Public Procurement Act 2007. Our notes set out what applies to mapping and drone survey work and what to ask any supplier for.

Nigerian content and procurement notes

We respond to tenders, RFQs and RFPs. Send your supplier or prequalification forms with your request; the proposal states which registrations are in place for your contract and which are being arranged. Tell us the portal or format your process uses.

Frequently asked questions

Which widths do you measure in Nigeria?

The ones that apply to your asset. For power lines we default to the NESIS right of way for the voltage (50 m for 330 kV, 30 m for 132 kV, 11 m for 33 kV and 11 kV, split equally either side of the centre line). For pipelines we measure from the centreline you supply, from the boundary of the licence strip if you send it as a polygon, and to the distance in any Oil Pipelines Act s.12 order. Up to six widths can be reported in one survey.

Do you need anyone on site to start?

No. A survey starts from your route file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or imagery you already hold, so no one travels and no drone flies. That matters on swamp and creek stretches and where access is unsafe. Drone detail is added only where a stretch needs it, subject to the NCAA and ONSA authorisations each job requires.

Does this replace pipeline patrols or security contracts?

No. It shows your patrol, right-of-way and asset-protection teams where the ground has changed, so they go there first. AfriScan is a remote-sensing and mapping service, not a security service.

Can you detect taps, leaks or oil theft?

No. Imagery cannot see a tap, a leak or the condition of the pipe. We map what is visible at the surface, such as new structures, fresh digging, spoil, new tracks, cleared ground and visible signs of artisanal refining, and flag it for your teams to check.

Who sees our route and the results?

Only the contacts you name. We never publish maps of your assets or of the settlements around them without your written permission, military and other sensitive sites are masked, and the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 applies to any personal data in the imagery.

Can the register be shared with host communities or regulators?

That is your decision. The register records what stood where, and on which imagery date, so it can support community engagement, compensation enumeration, regulatory reporting and legal processes. Whether a structure is authorised is for you and the authorities to decide, not for us.

Know what stands on your right of way before it becomes a claim.

Send the route (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage) or the licence strip as a polygon, the state or states it crosses, and the widths that matter: the NESIS width for the voltage, an Oil Pipelines Act order, or your company standard. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
